entries.67a043ed7215b2b524d960464721652f86f1af73: <div sID="gen12342" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="104" osisID="Ps.104" sID="Ps.104"/> <div eID="gen12342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12343" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12344" type="x-p"/> It is very probable that this psalm was penned by the same hand, and at the same time, as the former; for as that ended this begins, with "Bless the Lord, O my soul!" and concludes with it too. The style indeed is somewhat different, because the matter is so: the scope of the foregoing psalm was to celebrate the goodness of God and his tender mercy and compassion, to which a soft and sweet style was most agreeable; the scope of this is to celebrate his greatness, and majesty, and sovereign dominion, which ought to be done in the most stately lofty strains of poetry. David, in the former psalm, gave God the glory of his covenant-mercy and love to his own people; in this he gives him the glory of his works of creation and providence, his dominion over, and his bounty to, all the creatures. God is there praised as the God of grace, here as the God of nature. And this psalm is wholly bestowed on that subject; not as <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Ps. xix.</reference>, which begins with it, but passes from it to the consideration of the divine law; nor as <reference osisRef="Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9">Ps. viii.</reference>, which speaks of this but prophetically, and with an eye to Christ. This noble poem is thought by very competent judges greatly to excel, not only for piety and devotion (that is past dispute), but for flight of fancy, brightness of ideas, surprising turns, and all the beauties and ornaments of expression, the Greek and Latin poets upon any subject of this nature. Many great things the psalmist here gives God the glory of I. The splendour of his majesty in the upper world, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.1-Ps.104.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The creation of the sea and the dry land, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.5-Ps.104.9">ver. 5-9</reference>. III. The provision he makes for the maintenance of all the creatures according to their nature, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.10-Ps.104.18">ver. 10-18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.27">27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.28">28</reference>. IV. The regular course of the sun and moon, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.19-Ps.104.24">ver. 19-24</reference>. V. The furniture of the sea, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.25-Ps.104.26">ver. 25, 26</reference>. IV. God's sovereign power over all the creatures, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.29-Ps.104.32">ver. 29-32</reference>. And, lastly, he concludes with a pleasant and firm resolution to continue praising God (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.33-Ps.104.35">ver. 33-35</reference>), with which we should heartily join in singing this psalm.
entries.df1aaf0725bac1daad28ca9026a348847c93e9fe: <div eID="gen12344" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12343" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Majesty.</title> <div sID="gen12345" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O my soul<hi type="small-caps">. O Lord</hi> my God, thou art very great; thou art clothed with honour and majesty. <hi type="super">2</hi> Who coverest <hi type="italic">thyself</hi> with light as <hi type="italic">with</hi> a garment: who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain: <hi type="super">3</hi> Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind: <hi type="super">4</hi> Who maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire: 5 <hi type="italic">Who</hi> laid the foundations of the earth, <hi type="italic">that</hi> it should not be removed for ever. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou coveredst it with the deep as <hi type="italic">with</hi> a garment: the waters stood above the mountains. 7 At thy rebuke they fled; at the voice of thy thunder they hasted away. <hi type="super">8</hi> They go up by the mountains; they go down by the valleys unto the place which thou hast founded for them. <hi type="super">9</hi> Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again to cover the earth. <div eID="gen12345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12346" type="x-p"/> When we are addressing ourselves to any religious service we must <hi type="italic">stir up ourselves to take hold on God</hi> in it (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.7">Isa. lxiv. 7</reference>); so David does here. "Come, my soul, where art thou? What art thou thinking of? Here is work to be done, good work, angels' work; set about it in good earnest; let all the powers and faculties be engaged and employed in it: <hi type="italic">Bless the Lord, O my soul!</hi>" In these verses, <div eID="gen12346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12347" type="x-p"/> I. The psalmist looks up to the divine glory shining in the upper world, of which, though it is one of the things not seen, faith is the evidence. With what reverence and holy awe does he begin his meditation with that acknowledgment: <hi type="italic">O Lord my God! thou art very great!</hi> It is the joy of the saints that he who is their God is a great God. The grandeur of the prince is the pride and pleasure of all his good subjects. The majesty of God is here set forth by various instances, alluding to the figure which great princes in their public appearances covet to make. Their equipage, compared with his (even of the eastern kings, who most affected pomp), is but as the light of a glow-worm compared with that of the sun, when he goes forth in his strength. Princes appear great, 1. In their robes; and what are God's robes? <hi type="italic">Thou art clothed with honour and majesty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.1">v. 1</reference>. God is seen in his works, and these proclaim him infinitely wise and good, and all that is great. Thou <hi type="italic">coverest thyself with light as with a garment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">v. 2</reference>. God <hi type="italic">is light</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.1.5">1 John i. 5</reference>), the <hi type="italic">Father of lights</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jam. i. 17</reference>); he <hi type="italic">dwells in light</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1 Tim. vi. 16</reference>); he clothes himself with it. The residence of his glory is in the highest heaven, that light which was created the first day, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.3">Gen. i. 3</reference>. Of all visible beings light comes nearest to the nature of a spirit, and therefore with that God is pleased to cover himself, that is, to reveal himself under that similitude, as men are seen in the clothes with which they cover themselves; and so only, for his face cannot be seen. 2. In their palaces or pavilions, when they take the field; and what is God's palace and his pavilion? He <hi type="italic">stretches out the heavens like a curtain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">v. 2</reference>. So he did at first, when he made the firmament, which in the Hebrew has its name from its being expanded, or <hi type="italic">stretched out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.1.7">Gen. i. 7</reference>. He made it to divide the waters as a curtain divides between two apartments. So he does still: he now <hi type="italic">stretches out the heavens like a curtain,</hi> keeps them upon the stretch, and they <hi type="italic">continue to this day according to his ordinance.</hi> The regions of the air are stretched out about the earth, like a curtain about a bed, to keep it warm, and drawn between us and the upper world, to break its dazzling light; for, though God <hi type="italic">covers himself with light,</hi> yet, in compassion to us, <hi type="italic">he makes darkness his pavilion. Thick clouds are a covering to him.</hi> The vastness of this pavilion may lead us to consider how great, how very great, he is that <hi type="italic">fills heaven and earth.</hi> He has his <hi type="italic">chambers,</hi> his <hi type="italic">upper rooms</hi> (so the word signifies), <hi type="italic">the beams</hi> whereof <hi type="italic">he lays in the waters,</hi> the waters that are above the firmament (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">v. 3</reference>), as he has <hi type="italic">founded the earth upon the seas and floods,</hi> the waters beneath the firmament. Though air and water are fluid bodies, yet, by the divine power, they are kept as tight and as firm in the place assigned them as a chamber is with beams and rafters. How great a God is he whose presence-chamber is thus reared, thus fixed! 3. In their coaches of state, with their stately horses, which add much to the magnificence of their entries; but God <hi type="italic">makes the clouds his chariots,</hi> in which he rides strongly, swiftly, and far above out of the reach of opposition, when at any time he will act by uncommon providences in the government of this world. He descended in a cloud, as in a chariot, to Mount Sinai, to give the law, and to Mount Tabor, to proclaim the gospel (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Matt. xvii. 5</reference>), and he <hi type="italic">walks</hi> (a gentle pace indeed, yet stately) <hi type="italic">upon the wings of the wind.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10-Ps.18.11">Ps. xviii. 10, 11</reference>. He commands the winds, directs them as he pleases, and serves his own purposes by them. 4. In their retinue or train of attendants; and here also God is very great, for (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.4">v. 4</reference>) he <hi type="italic">makes his angels spirits.</hi> This is quoted by the apostle (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.7">Heb. i. 7</reference>) to prove the pre-eminence of Christ above the angels. The angels are here said to be <hi type="italic">his angels</hi> and <hi type="italic">his ministers,</hi> for they are under his dominion and at his disposal; they are <hi type="italic">winds,</hi> and <hi type="italic">a flame of fire,</hi> that is, they appeared in wind and fire (so some), or they are as swift as winds, and pure as flames; or he <hi type="italic">makes them spirits,</hi> so the apostle quotes it. They are spiritual beings; and, whatever vehicles they may have proper to their nature, it is certain they have not bodies as we have. Being spirits, they are so much the further removed from the encumbrances of the human nature and so much the nearer allied to the glories of the divine nature. And they are bright, and quick, and ascending, as fire, as <hi type="italic">a flame of fire.</hi> In Ezekiel's vision they ran and returned <hi type="italic">like a flash of lightning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.14">Ezek. i. 14</reference>. Thence they are called <hi type="italic">seraphim—burners.</hi> Whatever they are, they are what God made them, what he still makes them; they derive their being from him, having the being he gave them, are held in being by him, and he makes what use he pleases of them. <div eID="gen12347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12348" type="x-p"/> II. He looks down, and looks about, to the power of God shining in this lower world. He is not so taken up with the glories of his court as to neglect even the remotest of his territories; no, not the sea and dry land. <div eID="gen12348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12349" type="x-p"/> 1. He has founded the earth, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.5">v. 5</reference>. Though he has <hi type="italic">hung it upon nothing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.2">Job xxvi. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">ponderibus librata suis—balanced by its own weight,</hi> yet it is as immovable as if it had been laid upon the surest foundations. He has built the earth upon her basis, so that though it has received a dangerous shock by the sin of man, and the malice of hell strikes at it, yet <hi type="italic">it shall not be removed for ever,</hi> that is, not till the end of time, when it must give way to the new earth. Dr. Hammond's paraphrase of this is worth noting: "God has fixed so strange a place for the earth, that, being a heavy body, one would think it should fall every minute; and yet, which way soever we would imagine it to stir, it must, contrary to the nature of such a body, fall upwards, and so can have no possible ruin but by tumbling into heaven." <div eID="gen12349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12350" type="x-p"/> 2. He has set bounds to the sea; for that also is his. (1.) He brought it within bounds in the creation. At first the earth, which, being the more ponderous body, would subside of course, was <hi type="italic">covered with the deep</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The waters were above the mountains;</hi> and so it was unfit to be, as it was designed, a habitation for man; and therefore, on the third day, God said, <hi type="italic">Let the waters under the heaven be gathered to one place, and let the dry land appear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.1.9">Gen. i. 9</reference>. This command of God is here called his <hi type="italic">rebuke,</hi> as if he gave it because he was displeased that the earth was thus covered with water and not fit for man to dwell on. Power went along with this word, and therefore it is also called here <hi type="italic">the voice of</hi> his <hi type="italic">thunder,</hi> which is a mighty voice and produces strange effects, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">At thy rebuke,</hi> as if they were made sensible that they were out of their place, <hi type="italic">they fled; they hasted away</hi> (they called, and not in vain, to the rocks and mountains to cover them), as it is said on another occasion (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">Ps. lxxii. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">The waters saw thee, O God! the waters saw thee; they were afraid.</hi> Even those fluid bodies received the impression of God's terror. But <hi type="italic">was the Lord displeased against the rivers?</hi> No; it was <hi type="italic">for the salvation of his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.8">Hab. iii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">13</reference>. So here; God rebuked the waters for man's sake, to prepare room for him; for <hi type="italic">men must not be made as the fishes of the sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">Hab. i. 14</reference>); they must have air to breathe in. Immediately therefore, with all speed, the waters retired, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.8">v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">They</hi> go over hill and dale (as we say), <hi type="italic">go up by the mountains</hi> and <hi type="italic">down by the valleys;</hi> they will neither stop at the former nor lodge in the latter, but make the best of their way <hi type="italic">to the place which thou hast founded for them,</hi> and there they make their bed. Let the obsequiousness even of the unstable waters teach us obedience to the word and will of God; for shall man alone of all the creatures be obstinate? Let their retiring to and resting in the place assigned them teach us to acquiesce in the disposals of that wise providence which appoints us the bounds of our habitation. (2.) He keeps it within bounds, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.9">v. 9</reference>. The waters are forbidden to pass over the limits set them; they may not, and therefore they do not, <hi type="italic">turn again to cover the earth.</hi> Once they did, in Noah's flood, because God bade them, but never since, because he forbids them, having promised not to drown the world again. God himself glorifies in this instance of his power (<reference osisRef="Job.38.8">Job xxxviii. 8</reference>, &c.) and uses it as an argument with us to fear him, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer. v. 22</reference>. This, if duly considered, would keep the world in awe of the Lord and his goodness, That the waters of the sea would soon cover the earth if God did not restrain them.
entries.360232b229b05c407dabf45b53cf26464bc9aa7d: <div eID="gen12350" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Bounty.</title> <div sID="gen12351" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> He sendeth the springs into the valleys, <hi type="italic">which</hi> run among the hills. <hi type="super">11</hi> They give drink to every beast of the field: the wild asses quench their thirst. 12 By them shall the fowls of the heaven have their habitation, <hi type="italic">which</hi> sing among the branches. <hi type="super">13</hi> He watereth the hills from his chambers: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works. <hi type="super">14</hi> He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth; <hi type="super">15</hi> And wine <hi type="italic">that</hi> maketh glad the heart of man, <hi type="italic">and</hi> oil to make <hi type="italic">his</hi> face to shine, and bread <hi type="italic">which</hi> strengtheneth man's heart. <hi type="super">16</hi> The trees of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> are full <hi type="italic">of sap;</hi> the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted; <hi type="super">17</hi> Where the birds make their nests: <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the stork, the fir trees <hi type="italic">are</hi> her house. <hi type="super">18</hi> The high hills <hi type="italic">are</hi> a refuge for the wild goats; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the rocks for the conies. <div eID="gen12351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12352" type="x-p"/> Having given glory to God as the powerful protector of this earth, in saving it from being deluged, here he comes to acknowledge him as its bountiful benefactor, who provides conveniences for all the creatures. <div eID="gen12352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12353" type="x-p"/> I. He provides fresh water for their drink: <hi type="italic">He sends the springs into the valleys,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.10">v. 10</reference>. There is water enough indeed in the sea, that is, enough to drown us, but not one drop to refresh us, be we ever so thirsty—it is all so salt; and therefore God has graciously provided water fit to drink. Naturalists dispute about the origin of fountains; but, whatever are their second causes, here is their first cause; it is God that <hi type="italic">sends the springs into the</hi> brooks, <hi type="italic">which</hi> walk by easy steps between <hi type="italic">the hills,</hi> and receive increase from the rain-water that descends from them. These <hi type="italic">give drink,</hi> not only to man, and those creatures that are immediately useful to him, but <hi type="italic">to every beast of the field</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.11">v. 11</reference>); for where God has given life he provides a livelihood and takes care of all the creatures. Even <hi type="italic">the wild asses,</hi> though untameable and therefore of no use to man, are welcome to <hi type="italic">quench their thirst;</hi> and we have no reason to grudge it them, for we are better provided for, though <hi type="italic">born like the wild ass's colt.</hi> We have reason to thank God for the plenty of fair water with which he has provided the habitable part of his earth, which otherwise would not be habitable. That ought to be reckoned a great mercy the want of which would be a great affliction; and the more common it is the greater mercy it is. <hi type="italic">Usus communis aquarum—water is common for all.</hi> <div eID="gen12353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12354" type="x-p"/> II. He provides food convenient for them, both for man and beast: <hi type="italic">The heavens drop fatness;</hi> they <hi type="italic">hear the earth,</hi> but God <hi type="italic">hears them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.21">Hos. ii. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">He waters the hills from his chambers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.13">v. 13</reference>), from those chambers spoken of (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">the beams of</hi> which <hi type="italic">he lays in the waters,</hi> those store-chambers, the clouds that distil fruitful showers. The hills that are not watered by the rivers, as Egypt was by the Nile, are watered by the rain from heaven, which is called <hi type="italic">the river of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.9">Ps. lxv. 9</reference>), as Canaan was, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.11-Deut.11.12">Deut. xi. 11, 12</reference>. Thus <hi type="italic">the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his works,</hi> either with the rain it drinks in (the earth knows when it has enough; it is a pity that any man should not) or with the products it brings forth. It is a satisfaction to the earth to bear the fruit of God's works for the benefit of man, for thus it answers the end of its creation. The <hi type="italic">food</hi> which God <hi type="italic">brings forth out of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">v. 14</reference>) is <hi type="italic">the fruit of his works,</hi> which <hi type="italic">the earth is satisfied with.</hi> Observe how various and how valuable its products are. <div eID="gen12354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12355" type="x-p"/> 1. For the cattle there is grass, and the beasts of prey, that live not on grass, feed on those that do; for man there is herb, a better sort of grass (and a dinner of herbs and roots is not to be despised); nay, he is furnished with <hi type="italic">wine, and oil, and bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">v. 15</reference>. We may observe here, concerning our food, that which will help to make us both humble and thankful. (1.) To make us humble let us consider that we have a necessary dependence upon God for all the supports of this life (we live upon alms; we are at his finding, for our own hands are not sufficient for us),—that our food comes all out of the earth, to remind us whence we ourselves were taken and whither we must return,—and that therefore we must not think to <hi type="italic">live by bread alone,</hi> for that will feed the body only, but must look into the word of God for the meat that endures to eternal life. Let us also consider that we are in this respect fellow-commoners with the beasts; the same earth, the same spot of ground, that brings grass for the cattle, brings corn for man. (2.) To make us thankful let us consider, [1.] That God not only provides for us, but for our servants. The cattle that are of use to man are particularly taken care of; grass is made to grow in great abundance for them, when <hi type="italic">the young lions,</hi> that are not for the service of man, often <hi type="italic">lack and suffer hunger.</hi> [2.] That our food is nigh us, and ready to us. Having our habitation on the earth, there we have our storehouse, and depend not on the <hi type="italic">merchant-ships that bring food from afar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.14">Prov. xxxi. 14</reference>. [3.] That we have even from the products of the earth, not only for necessity, but for ornament and delight, so good a Master do we serve. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Does nature call for something to support it, and repair its daily decays? Here is <hi type="italic">bread, which strengthens man's heart,</hi> and is therefore called <hi type="italic">the staff of life;</hi> let none who have that complain of want. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Does nature go further, and covet something pleasant? Here is <hi type="italic">wine, that makes glad the heart,</hi> refreshes the spirits, and exhilarates them, when it is soberly and moderately used, that we may not only go through our business, but go through it cheerfully. It is a pity that that should be abused to overcharge the heart, and unfit men for their duty, which was given to revive their heart and quicken them in their duty. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Is nature yet more humoursome, and does it crave something for ornament too? Here is that also out of the earth—<hi type="italic">oil to make the face to shine,</hi> that the countenance may not only be cheerful but beautiful, and we may be the more acceptable to one another. <div eID="gen12355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12356" type="x-p"/> 2. Nay, the divine providence not only furnishes animals with their proper food, but vegetables also with theirs (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The trees of the Lord are full of sap,</hi> not only men's trees, which they take care of and have an eye to, in their orchards, and parks, and other enclosures, but God's trees, which grow in the wildernesses, and are taken care of only by his providence; they <hi type="italic">are full of sap</hi> and want no nourishment. Even <hi type="italic">the cedars of Lebanon,</hi> an open forest, though they are high and bulky, and require a great deal of sap to feed them, have enough from the earth; they are trees <hi type="italic">which he has planted,</hi> and which therefore he will protect and provide for. We may apply this to the trees of righteousness, which are the planting of the Lord, planted in his vineyard; these <hi type="italic">are full of sap,</hi> for what God plants he will water, and those that <hi type="italic">are planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.92.13">Ps. xcii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen12356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12357" type="x-p"/> III. He takes care that they shall have suitable habitations to dwell in. To men God has given discretion to build for themselves and for the cattle that are serviceable to them; but there are some creatures which God more immediately provides a settlement for. 1. The birds. Some birds, by instinct, make their nests in the bushes near rivers (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">By the springs</hi> that <hi type="italic">run among the hills</hi> some of the <hi type="italic">fowls of heaven have their habitation, which sing among the branches.</hi> They sing, according to their capacity, to the honour of their Creator and benefactor, and their singing may shame our silence. Our <hi type="italic">heavenly Father feeds them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">Matt. vi. 26</reference>), and therefore they are easy and cheerful, and take no thought for the morrow. The birds being made to <hi type="italic">fly above the earth</hi> (as we find, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.20">Gen. i. 20</reference>), they <hi type="italic">make their nests</hi> on high, in the tops of trees (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.17">v. 17</reference>); it should seem as if nature had an eye to this in <hi type="italic">planting the cedars of Lebanon,</hi> that they might be receptacles for the birds. Those that fly heavenward shall not want resting-places. <hi type="italic">The stork</hi> is particularly mentioned; <hi type="italic">the fir-trees,</hi> which are very high, <hi type="italic">are her house,</hi> her castle. 2. The smaller sort of beasts (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The wild goats,</hi> having neither strength nor swiftness to secure themselves, are guided by instinct to <hi type="italic">the high hills,</hi> which are a refuge to them; and <hi type="italic">the rabbits,</hi> which are also helpless animals, find shelter in <hi type="italic">the rocks,</hi> where they can set the beasts of prey at defiance. Does God provide thus for the inferior creatures; and will he not himself be a refuge and dwelling-place to his own people?
entries.6b91f2eab1e27d550bbaee3b5dcfdf1038d1424c: <div eID="gen12357" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Bounty.</title> <div sID="gen12358" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou makest darkness, and it is night: wherein all the beasts of the forest do creep <hi type="italic">forth.</hi> 21 The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their meat from God. <hi type="super">22</hi> The sun ariseth, they gather themselves together, and lay them down in their dens. <hi type="super">23</hi> Man goeth forth unto his work and to his labour until the evening. 24 <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches. 25 <hi type="italic">So is</hi> this great and wide sea, wherein <hi type="italic">are</hi> things creeping innumerable, both small and great beasts. <hi type="super">26</hi> There go the ships: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> that leviathan, <hi type="italic">whom</hi> thou hast made to play therein. <hi type="super">27</hi> These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give <hi type="italic">them</hi> their meat in due season. <hi type="super">28</hi> <hi type="italic">That</hi> thou givest them they gather: thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good. <hi type="super">29</hi> Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. <hi type="super">30</hi> Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth. <div eID="gen12358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12359" type="x-p"/> We are here taught to praise and magnify God, <div eID="gen12359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12360" type="x-p"/> I. For the constant revolutions and succession of day and night, and the dominion of sun and moon over them. The heathen were so affected with the light and influence of the sun and moon, and their serviceableness to the earth, that they worshipped them as deities; and therefore the scripture takes all occasions to show that the gods they worshipped are the creatures and servants of the true God (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">He appointed the moon for seasons,</hi> for the measuring of the months, the directing of the seasons for the business of the husbandman, and the governing of the tides. The full and change, the increase and decrease, of the moon, exactly observe the appointment of the Creator; so does the sun, for he keeps as punctually to the time and place of his going down as if he were an intellectual being and knew what he did. God herein consults the comfort of man. 1. The shadows of the evening befriend the repose of the night (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou makes darkness and it is night,</hi> which, though black, contributes to the beauty of nature, and is as a foil to the light of the day; and under the protection of the night <hi type="italic">all the beasts of the forest creep forth</hi> to feed, which they are afraid to do in the day, God having put the <hi type="italic">fear</hi> and <hi type="italic">dread of man upon every beast of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.2">Gen. ix. 2</reference>), which contributes as much to man's safety as to his honour. See how nearly allied those are to the disposition of the wild beasts who <hi type="italic">wait for the twilight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.24.15">Job xxiv. 15</reference>) and have fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness; and compare to this the danger of ignorance and melancholy, which are both as darkness to the soul; when, in either of those ways, <hi type="italic">it is night,</hi> then <hi type="italic">all the beasts of the forest creep forth.</hi> Satan's temptations then assault us and have advantage against us. Then the <hi type="italic">young lions roar after their prey;</hi> and, as naturalists tell us, their roaring terrifies the timorous beasts so that they have not strength nor spirit to escape from them, which otherwise they might do, and so they become an easy prey to them. They are said to <hi type="italic">seek their meat from God,</hi> because it is not prepared for them by the care and forecast of man, but more immediately by the providence of God. The roaring of the young lions, like the crying of the young ravens, is interpreted <hi type="italic">asking their meat of God.</hi> Does God put this construction upon the language of mere nature, even in venomous creatures? and shall he not much more interpret favourably the language of grace in his own people, though it be weak and broken, <hi type="italic">groanings which cannot be uttered?</hi> 2. The light of the morning befriends the business of the day (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.22-Ps.104.23">v. 22, 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sun arises</hi> (for, as he <hi type="italic">knows his going down,</hi> so, thanks be to God, he knows his rising again), and then the wild beasts betake themselves to their rest; even they have some society among them, for they <hi type="italic">gather themselves together</hi> and <hi type="italic">lay down in their dens,</hi> which is a great mercy to the children of men, that while they are abroad, as becomes honest travellers, between sun and sun, care is taken that they shall not be set upon by wild beasts, for they are then drawn out of the field, and the sluggard shall have no ground to excuse himself from the business of the day with this, That there is <hi type="italic">a lion in the way.</hi> Therefore then <hi type="italic">man goes forth to his work and to his labour.</hi> The beasts of prey creep forth with fear; man goes forth with boldness, as one that has dominion. The beasts creep forth to spoil and do mischief; man goes forth to work and do good. There is the work of every day, which is to be done in its day, which man must apply to every morning (for the lights are set up for us to work by, not to play by) and which he must stick to till evening; it will be time enough to rest when the night comes, in which <hi type="italic">no man can work.</hi> <div eID="gen12360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12361" type="x-p"/> II. For the replenishing of the ocean (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.25-Ps.104.26">v. 25, 26</reference>): As <hi type="italic">the earth is full of God's riches,</hi> well stocked with animals, and those well provided for, so that it is seldom that any creature dies merely for want of food, <hi type="italic">so is this great and wide sea</hi> which seems a useless part of the globe, at least not to answer the room it takes up; yet God has appointed it its place and made it serviceable to man both for navigation (<hi type="italic">there go the ships,</hi> in which goods are conveyed, to countries vastly distant, speedily and much more cheaply than by land-carriage) and also to be his storehouse for fish. God made not the sea in vain, any more than the earth; he <hi type="italic">made it to be inherited,</hi> for <hi type="italic">there are things swimming innumerable, both small and great animals,</hi> which serve for man's dainty food. The whale is particularly mentioned in the history of the creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.21">Gen. i. 21</reference>) and is here called the <hi type="italic">leviathan,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job xli. 1</reference>. He is made to <hi type="italic">play in the sea;</hi> he has nothing to do, as man has, who <hi type="italic">goes forth to his work;</hi> he has nothing to fear, as the beasts have, that lie down in their dens; and therefore he plays with the waters. It is a pity that any of the children of men, who have nobler powers and were made for nobler purposes, should live as if they were sent into the world, like leviathan into the waters, to play therein, spending all their time in pastime. The leviathan is said to <hi type="italic">play in the waters,</hi> because he is so well armed against all assaults that he sets them at defiance and <hi type="italic">laughs at the shaking of a spear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.41.29">Job xli. 29</reference>. <div eID="gen12361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12362" type="x-p"/> III. For the seasonable and plentiful provision which is made for all the creatures, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.27-Ps.104.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. 1. God is a bountiful benefactor to them: He <hi type="italic">gives them their meat;</hi> he <hi type="italic">opens his hand and they are filled with good.</hi> He supports the armies both of heaven and earth. Even the meanest creatures are not below his cognizance. He is open-handed in the gifts of his bounty, and is a great and good housekeeper that provides for so large a family. 2. They are patient expectants from him: They <hi type="italic">all wait upon him.</hi> They seek their food, according to the natural instinct God has put into them and in the proper season for it, and affect not any other food, or at any other time, than nature has ordained. They do their part for the obtaining of it: what God gives them <hi type="italic">they gather,</hi> and expect not that Providence should put it into their mouths; and what they gather they are satisfied with—<hi type="italic">they are filled with good.</hi> They desire no more than what God sees fit for them, which may shame our murmurings, and discontent, and dissatisfaction with our lot. <div eID="gen12362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12363" type="x-p"/> IV. For the absolute power and sovereign dominion which he has over all the creatures, by which every species is still continued, though the individuals of each are daily dying and dropping off. See here, 1. All the creatures perishing (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hidest thy face,</hi> withdrawest thy supporting power, thy supplying bounty, and <hi type="italic">they are troubled</hi> immediately. Every creature has as necessary a dependence upon God's favours as every saint is sensible he has and therefore says with David (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Ps. xxx. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou didst hide thy face and I was troubled.</hi> God's displeasure against this lower world for the sin of man is the cause of all the vanity and burden which the whole creation groans under. <hi type="italic">Thou takest away their breath,</hi> which is in thy hand, and then, and not till then, <hi type="italic">they die and return to their dust,</hi> to their first principles. The <hi type="italic">spirit of the beast, which goes downward,</hi> is at God's command, as well as <hi type="italic">the spirit of a man, which goes upward.</hi> The death of cattle was one of the plagues of Egypt, and is particularly taken notice of in the drowning of the world. 2. All preserved notwithstanding, in a succession (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created.</hi> The same spirit (that is, the same divine will and power) by which they were all created at first still preserves the several sorts of creatures in their being, and place, and usefulness; so that, though one generation of them passes away, another comes, and from time to time they are created; new ones rise up instead of the old ones, and this is a continual creation. Thus the <hi type="italic">face of the earth is renewed</hi> from day to day by the light of the sun (which beautifies it anew every morning), from year to year by the products of it, which enrich it anew every spring and put quite another face upon it from what it had all winter. The world is as full of creatures as if none died, for the place of those that die is filled up. This (the Jews say) is to be applied to the resurrection, which every spring is an emblem of, when a new world rises out of the ashes of the old one. <div eID="gen12363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12364" type="x-p"/> In the midst of this discourse the psalmist breaks out into wonder at the works of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">O Lord! how manifold are thy works!</hi> They are numerous, they are various, of many kinds, and many of every kind; and yet <hi type="italic">in wisdom hast thou made them all.</hi> When men undertake many works, and of different kinds, commonly some of them are neglected and not done with due care; but God's works, though many and of very different kinds, are all made in wisdom and with the greatest exactness; there is not the least flaw nor defect in them. The works of art, the more closely they are looked upon with the help of microscopes, the more rough they appear; the works of nature through these glasses appear more fine and exact. They are all made in wisdom, for they are all made to answer the end they were designed to serve, the good of the universe, in order to the glory of the universal Monarch.
entries.8d27c8eba22f4b19f5d0d77a091fe79a2185f4e3: <div eID="gen12364" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Bounty.</title> <div sID="gen12365" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall endure for ever: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall rejoice in his works. <hi type="super">32</hi> He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth: he toucheth the hills, and they smoke. <hi type="super">33</hi> I will sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> as long as I live: I will sing praise to my God while I have my being. <hi type="super">34</hi> My meditation of him shall be sweet: I will be glad in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 35 Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless thou the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O my soul. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> The psalmist concludes this meditation with speaking, <div eID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12367" type="x-p"/> I. Praise to God, which is chiefly intended in the psalm. <div eID="gen12367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> 1. He is to be praised, (1.) As a great God, and a God of matchless perfection: <hi type="italic">The glory of the Lord shall endure for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.31">v. 31</reference>. It shall endure to the end of time in his works of creation and providence; it shall endure to eternity in the felicity and adorations of saints and angels. Man's glory is fading; God's glory is everlasting. Creatures change, but with the Creator there is no variableness. (2.) As a gracious God: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall rejoice in his works.</hi> He continues that complacency in the products of his own wisdom and goodness which he had when he <hi type="italic">saw every thing that he had made, and behold it was very good,</hi> and <hi type="italic">rested the seventh day.</hi> We often do that which, upon the review, we cannot rejoice in, but are displeased at, and wish undone again, blaming our own management. But God always <hi type="italic">rejoices in his works,</hi> because they are all done in wisdom. We regret our bounty and beneficence, but God never does; he rejoices in the works of his grace: his <hi type="italic">gifts and callings</hi> are <hi type="italic">without repentance.</hi> (3.) As a God of almighty power (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">He looks on the earth, and it trembles,</hi> as unable to bear his frowns—trembles, as Sinai did, <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord. He touches the hills, and they smoke.</hi> The volcanoes, or burning mountains, such as Ætna, are emblems of the power of God's wrath fastening upon proud unhumbled sinners. If an angry look and a touch have such effects, what will the weight of his heavy hand do and the operations of his outstretched arm? <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of his anger?</hi> Who then dares set it at defiance? God rejoices in his works because they are all so observant of him; and he will in like manner <hi type="italic">take pleasure in those that fear him and that tremble at his word.</hi> <div eID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12369" type="x-p"/> 2. The psalmist will himself be much in praising him (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.33">v. 33</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will sing unto the Lord, unto my God,</hi> will praise him as Jehovah, the Creator, and as <hi type="italic">my God,</hi> a God in covenant with me, and this not now only, but <hi type="italic">as long as I live,</hi> and <hi type="italic">while I have my being.</hi>" Because we have our being from God, and depend upon him for the support and continuance of it, as long as we live and have our being we must continue to praise God; and when we have no life, no being, on earth, we hope to have a better life and better being in a better world and there to be doing this work in a better manner and in better company. <div eID="gen12369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12370" type="x-p"/> II. Joy to himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">My meditation of him shall be sweet;</hi> it shall be fixed and close; it shall be affecting and influencing; and therefore it shall be sweet. Thoughts of God will <hi type="italic">then</hi> be most pleasing, when they are most powerful. Note, Divine meditation is a very sweet duty to all that are sanctified: "<hi type="italic">I will be glad in the Lord;</hi> it shall be a pleasure to me to praise him; I will be glad of all opportunities to set forth his glory; and I will <hi type="italic">rejoice in the Lord always</hi> and in him only." All my joys shall centre in him, and in him they shall be full. <div eID="gen12370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12371" type="x-p"/> III. Terror to the wicked (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth; and let the wicked be no more.</hi> 1. Those that oppose the God of power, and fight against him, will certainly be consumed; none can prosper that harden themselves against the Almighty. 2. Those that rebel against the light of such convincing evidence of God's being, and refuse to serve him whom all the creatures serve, will justly be consumed. Those that make that earth to groan under the burden of their impieties which God thus fills with his riches deserve to be consumed out of it, and that it should spue them out. 3. Those that heartily desire to praise God themselves cannot but have a holy indignation at those that blaspheme and dishonour him, and a holy satisfaction in the prospect of their destruction and the honour that God will get to himself upon them. Even this ought to be the matter of their praise: "While <hi type="italic">sinners</hi> are <hi type="italic">consumed out of the earth,</hi> let <hi type="italic">my soul bless the Lord</hi> that I am not cast away with the workers of iniquity, but distinguished from them by the special grace of God. When <hi type="italic">the wicked</hi> are <hi type="italic">no more</hi> I hope to be praising God world without end; and therefore, <hi type="italic">Praise you the Lord;</hi> let all about me join with me in praising God. <hi type="italic">Hallelujah;</hi> sing praise to Jehovah." This is the first time that we meet with <hi type="italic">Hallelujah;</hi> and it comes in here upon occasion of the destruction of the wicked; and the last time we meet with it is upon a similar occasion. When the New-Testament Babylon is consumed, this is the burden of the song, <hi type="italic">Hallelujah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">Rev. xix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.3">3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.4">4,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">6</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.104"/> <div eID="gen12371" type="x-p"/>

entries.46670d48f556f5525bac76b660c73bc391a9e94a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6689"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 104</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.104.1-Ps.104.35">Psa 104:1-35</reference>. The Psalmist celebrates God's glory in His works of creation and providence, teaching the dependence of all living creatures; and contrasting the happiness of those who praise Him with the awful end of the wicked.</title> <div sID="gen10245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6689"/>1. God's essential glory, and also that displayed by His mighty works, afford ground for praise. <div eID="gen10245" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5462ab6e42006ef7955253fa5767a28e0f0bbe1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6690"/><div sID="gen10246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6690"/><hi type="bold">2. light--</hi>is a figurative representation of the glory of the invisible God (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.2">Mt 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>). Its use in this connection may refer to the first work of creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.3">Ge 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen10246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stretchest out the heavens--</hi>the visible heavens or sky which cover the earth as a curtain (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Is 40:12</reference>). <div eID="gen10247" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7d479b79aaac37a6115931592c36ca9b530e0ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6691"/><div sID="gen10248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6691"/><hi type="bold">3. in the waters--</hi>or, it may be "with"; using this fluid for the beams, or frames, of His residence accords with the figure of clouds for chariots, and wind as a means of conveyance.<div eID="gen10248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walketh--</hi>or, "moveth" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">Psa 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.6">Am 9:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10249" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f0898c022d56b4f020c1428a75ee1f7fc9f56a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6692"/><div sID="gen10250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6692"/>4. This is quoted by Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.7">He 1:7</reference>) to denote the subordinate position of angels; that is, they are only messengers as other and material agencies.<div eID="gen10250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirits--</hi>literally, "winds."<div eID="gen10251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flaming fire--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.105.32">Psa 105:32</reference>) being here so called. <div eID="gen10252" type="x-p"/>
entries.1deb1cdea6f82c06b737fb13c3738557dc8a562f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6693"/><div sID="gen10253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6693"/>5. The earth is firmly fixed by His power. <div eID="gen10253" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e9b7cb7ba11a7ba8a98da9e3e634e3fcc0928bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6694"/><div sID="gen10254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6694"/>6-9. These verses rather describe the wonders of the flood than the creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.19">Ge 7:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5">2Pe 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.6">6</reference>). God's method of arresting the flood and making its waters subside is poetically called a "rebuke" (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Is 50:2</reference>), and the process of the flood's subsiding by undulations among the hills and valleys is vividly described. <div eID="gen10254" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c701c5d9cffbcffee8ee5808cb10a682caedac7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6695"/><div sID="gen10255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6695"/>10-13. Once destructive, these waters are subjected to the service of God's creatures. In rain and dew from His chambers (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>), and fountains and streams, they give drink to thirsting animals and fertilize the soil. Trees thus nourished supply homes to singing birds, and the earth teems with the productions of God's wise agencies, <div eID="gen10255" type="x-p"/>
entries.40c79cd0b0bf6e014cc3cd5377a54ecc45672d69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6696"/><div sID="gen10256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6696"/>14-15. so that men and beasts are abundantly provided with food.<div eID="gen10256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the service--</hi>literally, "for the culture," &c., by which he secures the results.<div eID="gen10257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oil ... shine--</hi>literally, "makes his face to shine more than oil," that is, so cheers and invigorates him, that outwardly he appears better than if anointed.<div eID="gen10258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strengtheneth ... heart--</hi>gives vigor to man (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.19.5">Jud 19:5</reference>). <div eID="gen10259" type="x-p"/>
entries.aee26e8848ddb65c2a2b1ee6ec1334585e130468: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6697"/><div sID="gen10260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6697"/>16-19. God's care of even wild animals and uncultivated parts of the earth. <div eID="gen10260" type="x-p"/>
entries.c792895c9ae92d73264dd2947832408530e58708: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6698"/><div sID="gen10261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6698"/>20-23. He provides and adapts to man's wants the appointed times and seasons. <div eID="gen10261" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6d3665e130d5c430af4c22567f25e0fee00d46c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6699"/><div sID="gen10262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6699"/>24-26. From a view of the earth thus full of God's blessings, the writer passes to the sea, which, in its immensity, and as a scene and means of man's activity in commerce, and the home of countless multitudes of creatures, also displays divine power and beneficence. The mention of <div eID="gen10262" type="x-p"/>
entries.17fcf50bdb7ca6002dbb28504582443b9752c118: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6701"/><div sID="gen10264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6701"/>27-30. The entire dependence of this immense family on God is set forth. With Him, to kill or make alive is equally easy. To hide His face is to withdraw favor (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.1">Psa 13:1</reference>). By His spirit, or breath, or mere word, He gives life. It is His constant providence which repairs the wastes of time and disease. <div eID="gen10264" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd9a043003aa43e6e01e5ab5dada64cb94f2480e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6702"/><div sID="gen10265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6702"/>31-34. While God could equally glorify His power in destruction, that He does it in preservation is of His rich goodness and mercy, so that we may well spend our lives in grateful praise, honoring to Him, and delightful to pious hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">Psa 147:1</reference>). <div eID="gen10265" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6eed6e0902a4cd6746ee73ab62e083546757407: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6703"/><div sID="gen10266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6703"/>35. Those who refuse such a protector and withhold such a service mar the beauty of His works, and must perish from His presence.<div eID="gen10266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Praise ye the Lord--</hi>The Psalm closes with an invocation of praise, the translation of a Hebrew phrase, which is used as an English word, "Hallelujah," and may have served the purpose of a chorus, as often in our psalmody, or to give fuller expression to the writer's emotions. It is peculiar to Psalms composed after the captivity, as "Selah" is to those of an earlier date. <chapter eID="Ps.104"/>

entries.1a4435ce338cf8ccb2f7981d62cdf7815ecb6acd: <div eID="gen22057" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22060" type="x-p"/> The majesty and power of God manifested in the creation of the heavens and the atmosphere, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.1-Psa.104.3">Psa 104:1-3</reference>; of the earth and sea, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.4-Psa.104.9">Psa 104:4-9</reference>; of the springs, fountains, and rivers, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.10-Psa.104.13">Psa 104:10-13</reference>; of vegetables and trees, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.14-Psa.104.18">Psa 104:14-18</reference>; of the sun and moon, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.19">Psa 104:19</reference>; of day and night, and their uses, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.20-Psa.104.23">Psa 104:20-23</reference>; of the riches of the earth, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.24">Psa 104:24</reference>; of the sea, its inhabitants, and its uses, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.25">Psa 104:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference>; of God's general providence in providing food for all kinds of animals, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.27-Psa.104.31">Psa 104:27-31</reference>; of earthquakes and volcanoes, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.32">Psa 104:32</reference>. God is praised for his majesty, and the instruction which his works afford, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.33">Psa 104:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.34">Psa 104:34</reference>. Sinners shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Psa.104.35">Psa 104:35</reference>. <div eID="gen22060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22061" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title either in the Hebrew or Chaldee; but it is attributed to David by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Syriac. It has the following title in the Septuagint, as it stands in the Complutensian Polyglot: Ψαλμος τῳ Δαυιδ ὑπερ της του κοσμου συστασεως "A Psalm of David concerning the formation of the world." The Syriac says it is "A Psalm of David when he went with the priests to adore the Lord before the ark." It seems a continuation of the preceding Psalm; and it is written as a part of it in nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. It is properly a poem on the works of God in the creation and government of the world; and some have considered it a sort of epitome of the history of the creation, as given in the book of Genesis. <div eID="gen22061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22063" type="x-p"/> O Lord my God, thou art very great - The works of God, which are the subject of this Psalm, particularly show the grandeur and majesty of God. The strongest proofs of the being of God, for common understandings, are derived from the works of creation, their magnitude, variety, number, economy, and use. And a proper consideration of those works presents a greater number of the attributes of the Divine nature than we can learn from any other source. Revelation alone is superior.
entries.8bc53f6b20263a30e0daae80a1d7f32b0a431791: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22064" type="x-p"/> Who coverest thyself with light - Light, insufferable splendor, is the robe of the Divine Majesty. Light and fire are generally the accompaniments of the Supreme Being, when he manifests his presence to his creatures. He appeared thus to Abraham when he made a covenant with him, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Gen 15:17</reference>; and to Moses when he appointed him to bring the people out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.3.2">Exo 3:2</reference>; and when he gave him his law on Sinai, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference>. Moses calls God a consuming fire, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.24">Deu 4:24</reference>. When Christ was transfigured on the mount, his face shone like the sun, and his garment was white as the light, <reference osisRef="Mat.17.2">Mat 17:2</reference>. And when the Lord manifests himself to the prophets, he is always surrounded with fire, and the most brilliant light. <div eID="gen22064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22065" type="x-p"/> Bishop Lowth has some fine remarks on the imagery and metaphors of this Psalm. The exordium, says he, is peculiarly magnificent, wherein the majesty of God is described, so far as we can investigate and comprehend it, from the admirable construction of nature; in which passage, as it was for the most part necessary to use translatitious images, the sacred poet has principally applied those which would be esteemed by the Hebrews the most elevated, and worthy such an argument; for they all, as it seems to me, are taken from the tabernacle. We will give these passages verbally, with a short illustration: - הוד והדר לבשת hod vehadar labashta. "Thou hast put on honor and majesty." <div eID="gen22065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22066" type="x-p"/> The original, לבשת, is frequently used when speaking of the clothing or dress of the priests. <reference osisRef="Psa.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference> עטה אור כשלמה oteh or cassalmah. "Covering thyself with light as with a garment." <div eID="gen22066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22067" type="x-p"/> A manifest symbol of the Divine Presence; the light conspicuous in the holiest is pointed out under the same idea; and from this single example a simile is educed to express the ineffable glory of God generally and universally. נוטה שמים כיריעה noteh shamayim kayeriah. "Stretching out the heavens like a curtain." <div eID="gen22067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22068" type="x-p"/> The word יריעה, rendered here curtain, is that which denotes the curtains or uncovering of the whole tabernacle. This may also be an allusion to those curtains or awnings, stretched over an area, under which companies sit at weddings, feasts, religious festivals, curiously painted under, to give them the appearance of the visible heavens in the night-season.
entries.cbfa7d77845622fe6ac6e084d4365927c9b1078b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> המקרה במים עליותיו hamekareh bammayim aliyothaiv. "Laying the beams of his chambers in the waters." <div eID="gen22068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22069" type="x-p"/> The sacred writer expresses the wonderful nature of the air aptly, and regularly constructed, from various and flux elements, into one continued and stable series, by a metaphor drawn from the singular formation of the tabernacle, which, consisting of many and different parts, and easily reparable when there was need, was kept together by a perpetual juncture and contignation of them all together. The poet goes on: - השם עבים רכובו hassem abim rechubo, המהלך על כנפי רוה hamehallech al canphey ruach. "Making the clouds his chariot, <div eID="gen22069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22070" type="x-p"/> Walking upon the wings of the wind." <div eID="gen22070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22071" type="x-p"/> He had first expressed an image of the Divine Majesty, such as it resided in the holy of holies, discernible by a certain investiture of the most splendid light; he now denotes the same from that light of itself which the Divine Majesty exhibited, when it moved together with the ark, sitting on a circumambient cloud, and carried on high through the air. That seat of the Divine Presence is even called by the sacred historians, as its proper name, המרכבה hammercabah, The Chariot.
entries.e76fd16a856c808cf50c28fa234579767dc802e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> עשה מלאכיו רחות oseh rnalachaiv ruchoth, משרתיו אש להט mesharethaiv esh lohet. <div eID="gen22071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22072" type="x-p"/> The elements are described as prompt and expedite to perform the Divine commands, like angels or ministers serving in the tabernacle; the Hebrew word משרתיו mesharethaiv being a word most common in the sacred ministrations.
entries.7b079a078de1da1e7e700f15035fe63d762a524a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> יסד ארץ על מכוניה yasad erets al mechonepha, בל תמוט עולם ועד bal tammot olam vaed. "Laying the earth upon its foundations, <div eID="gen22072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22073" type="x-p"/> That it should not be shaken for evermore." <div eID="gen22073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22074" type="x-p"/> This image Bishop Lowth thinks evidently taken from the tabernacle, which was so laid upon its foundations that nothing could move it, and the dispensation to which it was attached, till the end purposed by the secret counsel of God was accomplished: and thus the earth is established, till the end of its creation shall be fully answered; and then it and its works shall be burnt up. On the above ground, the stability of the sanctuary and the stability of the earth are sometimes mentioned in the same words.
entries.28f9f19cf08d8188ac4467d8900e59aa2b0c3151: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22075" type="x-p"/> Thou coveredst it with the deep - This seems to be spoken in allusion to the creation of the earth, when it was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the waters invested the whole, till God separated the dry land from them; thus forming the seas and the terraqueous globe. <div eID="gen22075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22076" type="x-p"/> The poet Ovid has nearly the same idea: - <div eID="gen22076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22077" type="x-p"/> Densior his tellus, elementaque grandia traxit, <div eID="gen22077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22078" type="x-p"/> Et pressa est gravitate sua; circumfluus humor <div eID="gen22078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22079" type="x-p"/> Ultima possedit, solidumque coercuit orbem. <div eID="gen22079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22080" type="x-p"/> Met. lib. i., ver. 29. <div eID="gen22080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22081" type="x-p"/> Earth sinks beneath, and draws a numerous throng <div eID="gen22081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22082" type="x-p"/> Of ponderous, thick, unwieldy seeds along: <div eID="gen22082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22083" type="x-p"/> About her coasts unruly waters roar; <div eID="gen22083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22084" type="x-p"/> And, rising on a ridge, insult the shore. <div eID="gen22084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22085" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.9d49f0d45804b64509904ca7e2f1e2cf65188a27: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22086" type="x-p"/> At thy rebuke they fled - When God separated the waters which were above the firmament from those below, and caused the dry land to appear. He commanded the separation to take place; and the waters, as if instinct with life, hastened to obey. <div eID="gen22086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22087" type="x-p"/> At the voice of thy thunder - It is very likely God employed the electric fluid as an agent in this separation.
entries.c45a4a4b4ddfd5022326af444cec4181ded0f9ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22088" type="x-p"/> They go up by the mountains; they go down by the valleys - Taking the words as they stand here, springs seem to be what are intended. But it is difficult to conceive how the water could ascend, through the fissures of mountains, to their tops, and then come down their sides so as to form rivulets to water the valleys. Most probably all the springs in mountains and hills are formed from waters which fall on their tops in the form of rain, or from clouds that, passing over them, are arrested, and precipitate their contents, which, sinking down, are stopped by some solid strata, till, forcing their way at some aperture at their sides, they form springs and fountains. Possibly, however, vapours and exhalations are understood; these by evaporation ascend to the tops of mountains, where they are condensed and precipitated. Thus the vapours ascend, and then come down to the valleys, forming fountains and rivulets in those places which the providence of God has allotted them; that is, continuous valleys, with such a degree of inclination as determines their waters to run in that direction till they reach another river, or fall into the ocean. <div eID="gen22088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22089" type="x-p"/> Some have thought there is a reference to the breaking up on the fountains of the great deep, at the time of the flood; while the protrusion of the waters would raise the circumambient crust, so as to form mountains, the other parts, falling in to fill up the vacuum occasioned by the waters which were thrown up from the central abyss, would constitute valleys. <div eID="gen22089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22090" type="x-p"/> Ovid seems to paraphrase this verse: - <div eID="gen22090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22091" type="x-p"/> Jussit et extendi campos, subsidere valles, <div eID="gen22091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22092" type="x-p"/> Fronde tegi sylvas, lapidosos surgere montes. <div eID="gen22092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22093" type="x-p"/> Met. lib. i., ver. 43. "He shades the woods, the valleys he restrains <div eID="gen22093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22094" type="x-p"/> With rocky mountains, and extends the plains." <div eID="gen22094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22095" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.b953eeda7e1783ca7023493f9a27c053a067cb13: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22096" type="x-p"/> Thou hast set a bound that they may not pass - And what is this bound? The flux and reflux of the sea, occasioned by the solar and lunar attraction, the rotation of the earth on its own axis, and the gravitation of the waters to the center of the earth. And what is the cause of all these? The will and energy of God. Thus the sea is prevented from drowning the earth equally where there are flat shores as where the sea seems hemmed in by huge mounds of land and mountains. The above, not these, are the bounds which it cannot pass, so that they cannot turn again to cover the earth.
entries.a47e7826bb5da9c78749a43f176c6807c93ae152: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22097" type="x-p"/> He sendeth the springs into the valleys - Evaporation is guided and regulated by Divine Providence. The sun has a certain power to raise a certain portion of vapours from a given space. God has apportioned the aqueous to the terrene surface, and the solar attraction to both. There is just as much aqueous surface as affords a sufficiency of vapours to be raised by the solar attraction to water the earthy surface. Experiments have been instituted which prove that it requires a given space of aqueous surface to provide vapours for a given space of terrene surface; and the proportion appears ordinarily to be seventeen of water to three of earth; and this is the proportion that the aqueous bears to the terrene surface of the globe. See Ray's three Physico-theological Discourses.
entries.63e42ee84e3ee3241b45a61606434f9fc8027737: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen22097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22098" type="x-p"/> The wild asses quench their thirst - The פרא pere, onager or wild ass, differs in nothing from the tame ass, only it has not a broken spirit, and is consequently more lively and active. It is so very swift that no horse except the Arab barb can overtake it. It is a gregarious animal, and they go in troops to feed and to drink. It is very timid, or rather jealous of its liberty, and therefore retires deep into the desert; yet even there the providence of God regards it; springs are provided, and it has the instinct to find them out.
entries.a7f7c6ac1a9197b9ed72b24d3a3c9caf828371aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22099" type="x-p"/> By them shall the fowls of the heaven have their habitation - All fowls love verdure, and have their residence where they can find wood and water.
entries.7b38e72659126dc9bad5ade63ed0c7c0c7278a6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22100" type="x-p"/> From his chambers - The clouds, as in <reference osisRef="Psa.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>. <div eID="gen22100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22101" type="x-p"/> The earth is satisfied - The inhabitants of it.
entries.fcead5e96adee0ea307b5d83e80fdd71e09487ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen22101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22102" type="x-p"/> He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle - Doth God care for oxen? Yes, and there is not a beast of the field that does not share his merciful regards. <div eID="gen22102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22103" type="x-p"/> And herb for the serviee of man - Plants, esculent herbs, and nutritive grain in general; and thus he brings forth food (לחם lechem, bread) out of the earth. In the germination and growth of a grain of wheat there is a profusion of miracles. God takes care of man, and of all those animals which are so necessary to the convenience and comfort of man.
entries.e98f963125202da63bb1d1a6c40ca242b3187c15: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22104" type="x-p"/> And wine - Wine, in moderate quantity, has a wondrous tendency to revive and invigorate the human being. Ardent spirits exhilarate, but they exhaust the strength; and every dose leaves man the worse. Unadulterated wine, on the contrary, exhilarates and invigorates: it makes him cheerful, and provides for the continuance of that cheerfulness by strengthening the muscles, and bracing the nerves. This is its use. Those who continue drinking till wine inflames them, abase this mercy of God. <div eID="gen22104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22105" type="x-p"/> Oil to make his face to shine - That is, to anoint the body; and particularly those parts most exposed to the sun and weather. This is of high importance in all arid lands and sultry climates. By it the pores are kept open, and perspiration maintained. <div eID="gen22105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22106" type="x-p"/> Bread which strengtheneth man's heart - In hunger not only the strength is prostrated, but the natural courage is also abated. Hunger has no enterprise, emulation, nor courage. But when, in such circumstances, a little bread is received into the stomach, even before concoction can have time to prepare it for nutriment, the strength is restored, and the spirits revived. This is a surprising effect; and it has not yet been satisfactorily accounted for. <div eID="gen22106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22107" type="x-p"/> Three of the choicest and most important articles of life are here mentioned: Wine, for the support of the vital and intellectual spirits; Bread, for the support of the nervous and muscular system; and Oil, as a seasoner of food, and for those unctions so necessary for the maintenance of health. Where wine, oil, and bread can be had in sufficient quantities, there animal food, ardent spirits, and all high-seasoned aliments, may be well dispensed with. Heavy taxes on these necessaries of life are taxes on life, itself; and infallibly lead to adulteration of the articles themselves; especially wine and oil, which, in countries where they are highly taxed, are no longer to be found pure.
entries.a6c0cd858f34b66e2dda0b9fded382eb6d87d4ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22108" type="x-p"/> The trees of the Lord are full of sap - ישבעו yisbeu, "are saturated." <div eID="gen22108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22109" type="x-p"/> The cedars of Lebanon - God's providence not only extends to then and cattle, but also to the trees of the field and forest. Many of these are not only sustained, but planted by his providence. Who ever planted the seeds of the cedars of Lebanon, or of the thousands of woods and forests on the globe? God himself sowed those seeds, and they have sprung up and flourished without the care of man.
entries.58a3e9b85fe113092dd41c167de416122a40b552: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22110" type="x-p"/> Where the birds make their nests - צפרים tsipporim signifies swallows, sparrows, and small birds in general; here opposed to the חסידה chasidah or stork. Perhaps the heron may be understood, which is said to be the first of all birds to build her nest, and she builds it on the very highest trees. The general meaning is, that God has provided shelter and support for the greatest and smallest birds; they are all objects of his providential regard.
entries.f9760fe5d9c4889a69de75bf58234c54b7c2ea10: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen22110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22111" type="x-p"/> The high hills are a refuge - The barren tops of the highest hills, and the craggy abrupt precipices of the most stupendous rocks, are not without their uses: they afford protection, refuge, and food, for creatures whose dispositions and habits are suited to such places; and thus no part of the creation is useless. The creatures who are their inhabitants are necessary links in the great chain of animated beings, and show the wisdom and providence of God. <div eID="gen22111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22112" type="x-p"/> For a description of the covey, see <reference osisRef="Lev.11.5">Lev 11:5</reference>. The יעל yael, translated here the wild goat, is no doubt a creature of the stag or deer kind; the ibex, chamois, antelope, etc.
entries.0176aacc8d6b685e2a9ab485244e95c7766c7a82: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22113" type="x-p"/> He appointed the moon for seasons - The heathens thought that the sun and moon were gods, and worshipped them as such. The psalmist shows, 1. That they are creatures dependent on God for their being and continuance; and, 2. That they were made for the use of man. See what has been said on these luminaries in the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.1.14-Gen.1.16">Gen 1:14-16</reference> (note).
entries.e5404d666019ac9b1fe4757aee89d631522dd7da: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen22113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22114" type="x-p"/> Thou makest darkness - It is not the design of God that there should be either constant darkness or constant light. That man may labor, he gives him, by means of the sun, the light of the day; and that he may rest from his labor, and get his strength recruited, he gives him night, and comparative darkness. And as it would not be convenient for man and the wild beasts of the forest to collect their food at the same time, he has given the night to them as the proper time to procure their prey, and the day to rest in. When Man labors, They rest; when Man rests, They labor.
entries.f95b38e4a6a038f7df30476a88053f95af76ee4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen22114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22115" type="x-p"/> The young lions roar after their prey - It is said of the lion, that his roaring is so terrible as to astonish and quite unnerve the beast which he pursues; so that, though fleeter than himself, it falls down and becomes an easy prey.
entries.96a8d449c328322b8342aeb2bd4d690b09beb1a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen22115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22116" type="x-p"/> The sun ariseth - The dawn of day is the warning for man to arise and betake himself to his work; and is the warning to them to retire to their dens.
entries.10b3d567ee1b321390464d3b6df2aeeef1357cb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen22116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22117" type="x-p"/> O Lord, how manifold are thy works - In this verse there are three propositions: <div eID="gen22117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22118" type="x-p"/> 1. The works of the Lord are multitudinous and varied. <div eID="gen22118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22119" type="x-p"/> 2. They are so constructed as to show the most consummate wisdom in their design, and in the end for which they are formed. <div eID="gen22119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22120" type="x-p"/> 3.
